1.pericope_label: Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father: for I was my father’s son, and he taught me

schools.summary: Henry applies the address to the teacher’s own family first and then to all young people, presses the duty of magistrates and ministers to instruct their own households, observes that only one son of Solomon’s is on record yet he taught other people’s children, cites Rehoboam against parents who despair, and guesses David was the stricter for having indulged Adonijah and Absalom.

Gill reports Gersom referring the father to God and Jarchi referring the sonship to God, and prefers Solomon and David in both places, takes the children for disciples rather than offspring, identifies the good doctrine as the Gospel, and makes the wisdom to be got Christ himself, possessed by faith.

Clarke frames the chapter as a preceptor telling his pupils how he was himself educated, outlines it in three parts, and ends with the maxim that teaching by precept and example together is best of all; Wesley glosses the father as the speaker himself, reads tender as young in years and tenderly bred, and assigns the following verses as far as the tenth to David.

Ellicott finds the notices of these early years agreeing with the historical books, identifies tender as the father’s own epithet, and traces the word for only through beloved as an only son to the Greek only-begotten and well-beloved applied to Christ; Keil and Delitzsch argue from the shift to the plural address that the poet is himself the son here instructed and deliberately avoids saying your father, and take the infinitive as design rather than object.

debates: Who is the father of the first verse? Gill reports Gersom taking it of God and himself prefers Solomon; Ellicott and Wesley gloss it simply as the teacher speaking; Keil and Delitzsch make the deliberate avoidance of the phrase your father the proof that the teacher means himself, a father to his disciples and not the parent of any hearer; Henry allows both, addressing the teacher’s own children first and then all young people.

Whose son, and in what sense only? Gill reports Jarchi referring the sonship to God as father and answers that David is meant, adding that Solomon was not an only son but a darling; Ellicott concedes the plain fact that Bath-sheba had other children and saves the word by its history, only passing into beloved as an only son; Henry grounds the preference on the covenant being entailed, as with Isaac.
outliers: Wesley alone assigns the following verses, at least as far as the tenth, to David as the speaker, so that the chapter quotes a parent at length rather than paraphrasing him.

Ellicott carries the word for only out of the chapter altogether, through Isaac while Ishmael was living, to the Greek renderings only-begotten and well-beloved and their highest application to Christ.

Henry offers Rehoboam as consolation to parents whose children disappoint their education, and observes that thousands have got more good from these proverbs than the son to whom they seem to have been dedicated.
Henry guesses that David was the stricter with this son because he had seen the effects of never crossing Adonijah in anything, and of Absalom.
themes: a teacher who is a father only by discipleship
a grammar shift used as evidence of who is speaking
an only son who was not an only child
instruction remembered and repeated a generation later
precept and example weighed against each other

6.pericope_label: Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: exalt her, and she shall promote thee

schools.summary: Gill reads the whole passage of Christ, listing the ways wisdom may be forsaken and distinguishing nominal professors who forsake finally from believers who forsake for a time, piling up titles to show the principal thing is the principal person, reporting the Talmudists on exalt as a diligent search, and taking the ornament as justifying and sanctifying grace.

Clarke renders the opening words as wisdom is the principle, makes the knowledge of God the leaping point of religion, assembles a textual dossier of Coverdale, an old manuscript Bible, the Arabic, the Septuagint and the Complutensian Polyglot, distinguishes wisdom from understanding in a series of antitheses, and quotes the aphorism that knowledge is power; Wesley glosses exalting as highest esteem and keeps the ornament literal.

Ellicott offers the alternative rendering that makes the beginning of wisdom consist in getting wisdom at the price of all one has, and matches the eighth verse with the promise that those who honour God are honoured; Keil and Delitzsch argue the same rendering from the position of the subject against the motto of the book, fix the sense of the word for exalt from its parallel and from a buyer raising his offer, reject the Greek walling as unsuitable, note the transposition of performance and consequence, and deny that the father has stopped speaking.

debates: How should the seventh verse be rendered? Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both take it as the beginning of wisdom is, Get wisdom, with understanding bought at the price of everything one has, Keil and Delitzsch arguing it from the position of the subject as against the motto of the book; Clarke keeps a declaration, wisdom is the principle, and Gill an assertion that wisdom is the principal thing, which he then reads of a person.

What does exalt mean here? Keil and Delitzsch treat the word as occurring only here, fix it from its parallel as a buyer raising his offer upon offer, and reject the Greek rendering that walls wisdom round as strange and unsuitable; Gill accepts a Greek sense of the word, that of searching by turning things about, on the authority of the Talmudists.

Is the father still speaking at the tenth verse? Keil and Delitzsch deny against Hitzig that the admonition has passed over into the poet’s own warnings, holding that the instruction so far is general and the specific teaching still to come.
outliers: Clarke reports the whole seventh verse wanting in the Arabic and in the best copies of the Septuagint, and the Complutensian Polyglot reading understanding in place of wisdom in the first clause, so that the verse asks twice for the same thing.
Clarke separates wisdom from understanding in a run of antitheses: wisdom prescribes the end, understanding the ways and times; wisdom sees, understanding feels; one discovers, the other possesses.
Clarke warns that a sound creed is not enough, since devils believe and tremble, and that learning earns respect only where the learned man is consistent and not overbearing.
Keil and Delitzsch observe that the eighth verse transposes performance and consequence across its two clauses.
themes: a verse missing from two ancient witnesses
wisdom priced by a bidder raising his offer
the difference between seeing and feeling
a word read as searching and as walling round
an ornament taken literally and allegorically at once

10.pericope_label: Take fast hold of instruction: enter not into the path of the wicked; the path of the just is as the shining light

schools.summary: Henry reports and rejects the opinion that carries the father’s speech to the end of the chapter or of the ninth, presses the caution to a great distance rather than a due one and likens the company to a house of plague entered with an antidote, and insists the light of the just is a growing one, neither meteor nor candle but sunrise, perfect only in heaven.

Gill prefers the teacher to the father as the speaker here, takes the unstraitened steps of enemies and of saints brought into a large place, refuses the Latin rendering that forbids delighting in the way rather than entering it, reports Jarchi and Gersom making the verb mean destroy the way rather than flee it, and leaves the bread of wickedness open to both senses.

Clarke argues the long life medically from indolence and intemperance, reads the unstraitened steps as the clear way of an honest man of business, takes the sleeplessness literally of night robbery, resolves the bread and wine into stealing and highway robbery, and works out the optics of a sun still below the horizon whose rays reach us by the atmosphere; Wesley takes wickedness itself as their bread and the growing light as daily increase till glory.

Ellicott calls the practice of evil a second nature and makes the growing light the increasing knowledge of God; Keil and Delitzsch take the verb of avoiding in its fundamental sense of going aside, defend the marginal causative reading, argue from the parallel that the bread is bread got by wickedness rather than wickedness as bread, and propose that the verses on the two paths have been transposed.

debates: Whose words are these? Henry reports that some carry the father’s instructions to the end of the chapter and some as far as the end of the ninth, and prefers that the teacher resumes here if not sooner; Gill reports the same opinion and prefers the same answer, against Wesley earlier assigning at least the preceding verses to the father.

What is the bread of wickedness? Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch make it bread acquired by wickedness, Keil and Delitzsch arguing that the parallel word would have had to be different if wickedness itself were the food; Wesley takes it as wickedness being as pleasant to them as bread; Gill allows both senses without choosing; Clarke resolves the bread and the wine into private stealing and highway robbery.

What does the command to avoid the path require? Keil and Delitzsch make it spatial, going aside so as not to come to stand upon the way; Gill reports Jarchi and Gersom taking it as making the way void and hindering the wicked, and rejects the Latin rendering that forbids delighting in the way on the ground that delight presupposes the entry already forbidden.
outliers: Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch independently quote the same line of Virgil at the sleepless verse, Clarke as an address to an illnatured shepherd with a translation, Keil and Delitzsch as a grammatical parallel for the tense of the conditional clause.

Keil and Delitzsch judge it more probable that the verses on the shining path and the dark way have been transposed than that a conjunction stands out of its place, since the second joins the preceding verse without needing a particle at all.
Clarke grounds the promise of long life on physiology, deriving the principal part of our diseases from indolence, intemperance and disorderly passions, and crediting religion with preventing them.

Clarke reads the shining path as an account of refraction, the sun still below the horizon and his light reaching the earth through the atmosphere until the prepared day arrives at its determined time.
themes: a warning read as a plague house entered with an antidote
the same Latin poet quoted by two commentators at once
bread named from what buys it or from what it is
two verses suspected of having changed places
sunrise explained by the atmosphere

20.pericope_label: Keep thy heart with all diligence; ponder the path of thy feet, and turn not to the right hand nor to the left

schools.summary: Henry reports both senses of the word for keeping and ranks the heart above the eyes, tongue and feet, makes the words at once food and physic and a medicine for corruptions and grievances, weighs the path by putting the word of God in one scale and the action in the other, and closes with a Latin tag about keeping the eye on the goal.

Gill keeps the received rendering of the heart verse but adds that though kingdoms, cities, families and treasures are to be kept the heart is to be kept above all, reports Aben Ezra weighing the path in the balances of thought and the Greek making the paths straight instead, and takes the froward mouth of froward persons to be debarred good company.

Clarke renders the verse above all keeping, reads the issues of life as an allusion to the arteries carrying blood to the extremities and warns that the fountain must not be stopped up, makes the pondering deliberation before action, and assembles a full collation of the added verse the Greek and Latin carry, concluding it ancient and its promise true whether authentic or not; Wesley takes the heart as thoughts, will and affections and the pondering as consideration beforehand.

Ellicott renders the verse above all things to be guarded, lets the issues run to death as well as life, finds the word for froward to mean literally distortion, and makes the path to be levelled rather than pondered; Keil and Delitzsch settle the same rendering by grammar, describe the heart as the vessel of the blood-life that determines the direction life takes, argue at length that the verb means to clear a road and dismiss an Arabic parallel as unevidenced, and reject the added verse as an imitation betraying poverty of style.

debates: What does the verse about the path of the feet require? Gill, Henry, Clarke and Wesley all take it as pondering, weighing or considering, Henry making the scales explicit and Gill citing Aben Ezra for the balances; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both reject that sense outright for making the path smooth and level by removing obstacles, Keil and Delitzsch conceding that the verb once means to weigh out but insisting it everywhere else means to open a road.

How is the charge about the heart to be rendered? Clarke, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch all set aside diligence for above all keeping, or above all things that are to be guarded, Keil and Delitzsch deciding it by asking whether the noun names what is guarded against or the object of guarding; Henry reports both senses without choosing; Gill keeps diligence and smuggles the alternative in as a comment.

Is the verse the Greek and Latin add after the last one genuine? Clarke traces it through the versions, editions and manuscripts, notes that De Lyra rejects it as a gloss on no authority, and holds that even as an addition it is very ancient and its promise true; Keil and Delitzsch, having retranslated it into Hebrew, call it by no means genuine, since it takes right and left in a different sense from the verse it follows and promises as God’s work what the verse requires of man.
outliers: Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch independently read the issues of life as circulation, Clarke naming the arteries that carry blood to the utmost extremities and Keil and Delitzsch calling the heart the pitcher at the blood-fountain into which the blood also disembogues.
Keil and Delitzsch dismiss an Arabic word said to mean a balance, and printed in the newest editions of a standard lexicon, as devoid of all evidence.
Keil and Delitzsch report that Hitzig disputed the genuineness of the closing Hebrew verse itself, and defend it as continuing the preceding verse explanatorily rather than glossing it.
Henry takes the words as both food and physic, a medicine to all the flesh, meaning both the corruptions called flesh and the grievances that are as thorns in it.
themes: a verb that decides whether one weighs a road or levels it
the heart described as a pitcher at a fountain of blood
a verse present in two versions and absent from three
froward speech read as a mouth drawn awry
a single eye set against a squinting one
